ai.definition: Planetary-Scale Mycelial Soil Terraforming is a technology involving genetically engineered fungal networks designed to detoxify regolith and transform it into fertile soil on extraterrestrial bodies.
ai.howItWorks: The process involves deploying recursive symbiotic fungi clusters that can break down inorganic minerals, making them bio-available for plant growth. These fungi form extensive mycelial networks which spread through the regolith, converting it into a more hospitable environment for agriculture.
ai.problemSolved: This technology addresses the challenge of establishing sustainable agricultural practices on planets and moons with inhospitable or toxic soil conditions, such as those found in Mars' regolith or lunar dust (regolith).
ai.manufacturing: The manufacturing process involves cultivating genetically modified fungi strains under controlled conditions. These are then packaged into seed-like structures for deployment.
ai.buildProcess: Fungal spores are genetically engineered to enhance their detoxification and nutrient conversion capabilities. The resulting mycelium is grown in a sterile environment, dried, and encapsulated into lightweight, durable units designed for long-term space travel.
ai.costDrivers: Cost drivers include the initial genetic engineering of fungi strains, specialized cultivation facilities, and transportation costs associated with launching these units to distant planets or moons.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The technology is currently in the early stages of development but shows promise for future interplanetary colonization efforts.
ai.regulation: Currently, there are no specific regulations governing this technology. However, as it advances, environmental and safety standards will likely be established to ensure its responsible use.
ai.risks: Potential risks include unintended ecological impacts on alien worlds if the fungi escape or interact with native organisms in unexpected ways. Additionally, there is a risk of failure during deployment due to the complex nature of extraterrestrial environments.
ai.profitability: Profitability is speculative at this stage but could be significant for space agencies and private companies involved in interplanetary colonization efforts.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future development may focus on refining fungal strains, optimizing growth conditions, and developing more efficient delivery methods. Integration with other terraforming technologies could also enhance its effectiveness.
ai.energyRequirements: Field units draw low hundreds of watts; fabrication is energy-intensive due to vacuum baking but can be optimized through advanced manufacturing techniques.

glossary.def: The layer of loose, heterogeneous materials covering solid rock on terrestrial planets and moons.
The vegetative part of a fungus consisting of a mass of filaments called hyphae.
The process of altering the environment of an uninhabitable planet or moon to make it habitable for humans or other life forms.

subsystems.name: Inoculant organisms
subsystems.role: the fungi themselves — selected or engineered to grow on bare rock and mineral dust.
parts: mycorrhizal fungi that partner with plant roots
lichen symbioses of fungus plus alga

subsystems.name: Regolith conditioning
subsystems.role: makes crushed rock and dust habitable before biology can take hold.
parts: perchlorate and salt removal (a known hazard in Martian soil)

subsystems.name: Nutrient bridge
subsystems.role: adds the elements biology cannot mine from rock quickly.
parts: carbon source for the first generations

subsystems.name: Substrate engineering
subsystems.role: gives the network structure, moisture and gas exchange.

subsystems.name: Containment and monitoring
subsystems.role: keeps engineered organisms where they are meant to be.
parts: sensor network for temperature, moisture, chemistry

subsystems.name: Deployment system
subsystems.role: spreads and sustains inoculant over enormous areas.

buildSteps.title: Characterise the target ground
buildSteps.detail: Sample the regolith and measure its chemistry, grain size and toxicity. Martian soil is known to contain perchlorates, which are harmful to most life and must be dealt with first.

buildSteps.title: Select and engineer the organisms
buildSteps.detail: Screen fungi and lichens that already weather basalt and granite on Earth, then add tolerance to radiation, vacuum, desiccation and cold through selection or genetic engineering.

buildSteps.title: Leach and detoxify
buildSteps.detail: Wash or biologically reduce perchlorates and salts, and adjust pH, so the substrate stops being hostile.

buildSteps.title: Establish the first crust
buildSteps.detail: Lichens and free-living fungi are applied to moistened, amended regolith to start breaking minerals down into bio-available nutrients.

buildSteps.title: Add a nitrogen source
buildSteps.detail: Nitrogen is scarce in rock and absent from the atmosphere of Mars in usable form, so nitrogen-fixing microbes are introduced to build the nutrient pool.

buildSteps.title: Introduce plants and mycorrhizae
buildSteps.detail: Once organic matter and nutrients exist, plants are grown with fungal partners that trade minerals for sugars. Small plant-growth experiments in real lunar samples and regolith simulants are the earthly precursor to this step.

buildSteps.title: Scale in enclosed systems
buildSteps.detail: The whole cycle is repeated in sealed greenhouses, where failures stay contained and generations of organisms adapt.

buildSteps.title: Field trials
buildSteps.detail: Small plots are released under strict planetary-protection rules, monitored for spread and for whether soil depth and fertility actually keep increasing.

buildSteps.title: Recursive expansion
buildSteps.detail: Each plot becomes the nursery for the next, using locally grown inoculant and biomass rather than material shipped from Earth.

prerequisites.why: radiation- and desiccation-tolerant fungi and lichens exist, and lichens have survived Mars-like conditions in low Earth orbit, but no organism is engineered for planetary soil formation.
perchlorate removal and mineral weathering are demonstrated in the lab and in Mars simulants, never at landscape scale.
the ISS recycles water and some air, but no system has closed the nutrient loop through soil for years.

prerequisites.tech: In-situ resource use on another world
prerequisites.why: robots have made oxygen and water from local materials in experiments, but not soil at scale.
releasing engineered organisms on another world is a governance problem as much as a technical one.

pathway.milestone: lab and orbital tests of fungi, lichens and plants on regolith simulants and small amounts of real lunar material
pathway.unlocks: evidence about which organisms can survive and whether they release useful nutrients.

pathway.milestone: sealed greenhouse demonstrations on the Moon or Mars that cycle nutrients through soil for multiple seasons
pathway.unlocks: a working recipe for making topsoil from local rock.

pathway.milestone: contained hectare-scale plots with engineered inoculant and robotic tending
pathway.unlocks: real growth rates, spread control and soil-depth data.

pathway.milestone: open, self-spreading soil formation across a region
pathway.unlocks: agriculture and habitable landscapes at settlement scale — if containment, ethics and oversight can be settled first.
